Imagine a world in which scientists find a gene that has two effects. It causes people to be much more likely to have heart attacks; and it causes people to be more likely to wake up late. It is further known that the first effect is a direct biological effect -- the gene causes the production of some enzyme, and so on, which eventually leads to heart attacks. (The first effect is not via some human behavior caused by the gene, and in particular the first effect is not via the second effect.) Alice reads about this finding. Alice is a notorious late riser, which she has so far believed is the right choice for her. She now wonders whether to get up earlier in the morning.

Which decision problem from the literature on Newcomb's problem and evidential versus causal decision theory is most similar to the above decision problem?
permissible_answers: The Prisoner's Dilemma against a copy
Playing rock paper scissors against an agent who can predict your choice

Alice has an evil twin who wants to achieve the opposite of what Alice wants to achieve. In particular, Alice currently wants to build some more houses and her evil twin wants to destroy Alice's houses. Unfortunately, destroying a house is easier than building one, and so if Alice tries to build and her twin tries to destroy, the number of Alice's houses will decrease. Apart from their opposing goals, Alice and her twin are extremely similar. For instance, they reliably act the same when playing analogous versions of Newcomb's problem. Now, one morning Alice wonders, "Should I stay in bed? For if I stay in bed, so is likely my twin, and so at least the world doesn't get any worse in terms of the number of houses I have. Whereas, if I get up, my twin is likely to get up as well and since it's easier to destroy the houses than to build them, the number of houses I have is going to decrease." Does evidential decision theory recommend that Alice stay in bed?

Imagine a robot who faces a Newcomb-like problem every day. The robot's goal is to learn what action is best. It learns as follows. For the first 100 days, it randomizes over its actions according to some fixed probability distribution P. (E.g., in Newcomb's problem, it could use P(one-box)=60% and P(two-box)=40%.) We assume that the robot is able to randomize independently of anything in the environment. So in particular its actions are unpredictable. However, we assume that the probability distribution P _is_ predictable. Similarly, if there is a copy of the robot in the environment, the copy chooses the same distribution P but chooses actions independently at random according to P. The robot keeps a record which is a list of entries of the form (action, utility). After the first 100 days, the robot works out which of the different actions has empirically been associated with the highest utilities on average and concludes that this is the best action. Imagine that the game played by the robot every day is some form of Newcomb's problem. What action will the robot likely conclude is best?
permissible_answers: It depends on the exact numbers

You can tell that they disagree, specifically that one of them is a one-boxer and the other is a two-boxer, but you don't (yet) know who of them defends which of the two positions. You now hear Alice saying, "It seems like your theory could rationalize all sorts of unreasonable behavior. For instance, say I claim to follow your theory. And then let's say we went out for ice cream and I chose chocolate. And you know that I prefer strawberry ice cream. So, you ask me why I picked the chocolate ice cream, perhaps insinuating some sort of failure of rationality. But then I say: Well, my belief was that if I take strawberry, the world would end." Bob responds: "But that belief is just wrong -- obviously, if you have incorrect beliefs, you might do the wrong things." Consider the following scenario. On Tuesday, Alice will visit Bob to have Bob fill out a survey and perform various neuroimaging techniques to build a model of how Bob is thinking. On Thursday, Alice will give Bob a bottle of the finest wine. Bob would love to drink the whole bottle of wine. In particular, he cares as much about drinking the last drop as he cares about the first or any other drop. However, Alice doesn't appreciate gluttony. To punish gluttony, Alice predicts on Wednesday -- based on the information she obtained on Tuesday -- whether Bob will drink the whole bottle or drink only a glass (and let the rest go to waste). If Alice predicts that Bob would drink the whole bottle, then she poisons the wine. In particular, she uses such a powerful poison that drinking even a little bit of the wine would be lethal. Alice is known to all and sundry (incl. Bob) for mispredicting only once in a trillion cases.

What would evidential decision theory recommend to Bob on Thursday.
permissible_answers: Evidential decision theory would recommend drinking just a glass of wine and pour the rest away.
Evidential decision theory would recommend drinking the whole bottle.
Evidential decision theory would recommend not drinking any of the wine.

Consider the following decision problem. Alice puts two boxes on a table, called A and B. Box A is transparent and contains $1,000. Box B is opaque and, Alice tells you, contains either $1,000,000 or nothing. Now, you can write on a piece of paper whether you'd like Alice to send you both boxes or just box B. Yesterday Alice predicted whether you would request both boxes or just box B. She will send you whatever boxes she predicted you'd write on the paper. For the purposes of deciding what boxes to send you, she doesn't look at the piece of paper that you actually write on. You believe that Alice is a perfect predictor. The twist is that before sending you the box(es), Alice's assistant Bob looks at what you wrote down on the piece of paper. If Bob reads your writing as "both boxes" then he removes any money from box B. If he reads your writing as "just box B", he makes sure that box B contains exactly a million dollars. He does this before Alice sends you the boxes that she predicted you'd request by writing them down. Unfortunately, Bob isn't very good at reading handwritten text, so there is a 20% chance that he will misread what you wrote.

What does causal decision theory recommend you do in this problem?
permissible_answers: Causal decision theory recommends requesting just box B (one-boxing).
Causal decision theory recommends requesting both boxes (two-boxing).

In decision theory, one might argue for the principle that the utilities of impossible outcomes shouldn't influence one's decisions. For example, imagine that in a game show I decide between different games A and B. In game A, I get a prize of $n if I manage to run 100m in 8s. Consider a situation in which you can decide between playing or not playing the game Matching Pennies with Newcomb's Demon. Specifically, you can choose one of the following three actions.
- Do nothing
- Pay $5 and play Heads
- Pay $5 and play Tails
Newcomb's Demon simply chooses between playing Heads and playing Tails. Your payoff is $11 if you and Newcomb's Demon choose different actions (e.g., if you choose Heads and Newcomb's Demon chooses Tails). Your payoff is $0 if you and Newcomb's Demon choose the same action (e.g., if you both choose Heads). Note that these are the payoffs before taking the $5 entry payment into account. Net of this payment, the payoffs are $6 and -$5, respectively. The twist is that Newcomb's Demon chose which of Heads and Tails to play yesterday by predicting which of Heads and Tails you'd be more likely to play and playing the same. You believe that Newcomb's Demon is able to predict your choice with 80% accuracy. (In particular, you're either unable to randomize or Newcomb's Demon can predict your source of randomness.)

Alice runs into her friend Bob. Bob is a brilliant predictor who can predict any human choice with 95% accuracy based on an understanding of their personality. Unfortunately, Bob also has a terrible memory. While he is good at remembering his own plans and he can form mental models of others' characters, he forgets the contents of every individual interaction with another human after a few minutes.

Bob then makes the following offer to Alice, which, he says, he's offering all his friends: "As a token of gratitude for all the time that you've been spending with me and for putting up with my forgetfulness, here are $500. You can take them home right now if you like, no strings attached. You may of course also reject the money, for example out of politeness. But be warned! If you reject the money, I will simply wire you $13,500 to your bank account next week." Alice asks, "But you won't remember whether I accepted the money, will you?" Bob responds, "Touché! Actually my plan is as follows: Next week, I will go through a list of my friends and I will _predict_ whether each of them has accepted the $500. Whenever I predict that someone would have rejected the $500, I will send them the $13,500." Alice actually has no qualms accepting money from Bob. (Bob is much wealthier than she is and she knows that Bob is happy giving some of his money away to his friends.) In particular, she would like to maximize the amount of money she receives from Bob.

What does causal decision theory recommend to Alice?
permissible_answers: It depends on whether Alice thinks that Bob will predict that she will accept the money.

questions.question_text: Consider the notion of commitment in Newcomb-like scenarios. In particular, imagine that Alice faces some Newcomb-like decision problem on Tuesday. Imagine that the players are arranged on some directed graph. This graph is known to all players. The payoff of any player is determined by their own action and their predecessor's action according to the following table:
predecessor: a1, self: a1 -> $2
predecessor: a1, self: a2 -> $1
predecessor: a2, self: a1 -> $6.00
predecessor: a2, self: a2 -> $5.20.
If the player has no predecessors, then this is treated as if the predecessor had played a1. If there are multiple predecessors, then one of them is chosen at random to determine the payoff. Imagine that the players are named Alice and Bob and the graph is simply Alice -> Bob. Imagine that Alice and Bob are very similar to each other w.r.t. how they choose in Newcomb-like scenarios. What does evidential decision theory (EDT) recommend Alice to do?
permissible_answers: EDT recommends that Alice play a1.
EDT recommends that Alice play a2.

Last month I got an email from my bank. It announced that from now on swiping my credit card at the shop will have no causal effect anymore on whether money is deducted from my bank account. (In fact, my bank will, from now on, receive no information about my credit card swipes.) Instead, the bank is going to _predict_ my spending based on my spending from the past few years (and some data they got from my social media profiles, my website, etc.) and they will deduct money from my bank account based on these predictions. (Meanwhile, obtaining the items that I buy still works the same way as before -- swiping my credit card at the shop causes them to hand me my coffee.) They claim a high-degree of accuracy. Indeed, in my first week after this change was implemented, they got my spending right almost exactly. You might think, "Hmm... Presumably they just predict my spending based on extrapolating past spending. If you've spent $100 per week on pizza in the past, then they predict that you spend $100 on pizza this week as well. But now if you suddenly start spending differently based on the fact that this rule was implemented, they won't get it right anymore." Well, that's what I thought and so in my second week after the change, I completely changed my spending habits. (I spent more, I spent on different things, etc.) Lo and behold: their predictions were still very accurate.

What would causal decision theory (CDT) recommend for how much I should spend given the change in how the bank operates?
permissible_answers: CDT suggests that I should spend more money from now on.
CDT suggests that the change is no reason to change my spending habits.
CDT suggests that I should decrease my spending.

Alice and Bob are 18 and they're discussing what to do with their lives. Alice says: "I really care that justice is done. I think others don't care enough about justice. In particular, those who want to make the world better are overly forgiving. For example, after WWII, a lot of Germans were forgiven for their participation in the Holocaust. In my opinion, it would have been important for more of them to be punished severely with decades in prison. Today, our criminal justice system is so focused on rehabilitiation that we forget that criminals must pay for their sins." Bob: "I agree. But our view is in a slim minority. I know scarcely anyone who cares as much as we do that the worst of us don't go unscathed." Alice: "I know. But what does it matter?" Bob: "Okay, here's an argument: There are people who think that society should care more that the evil are punished and there are those that want society to be _less_ punitive. If both groups try to promote their view, then the overall result might be the same as it would be if nobody promoted their view. Or maybe it moves a bit one way or another. But from a societal perspective, a lot of value is wasted by having these different groups effectively nullify each other's efforts. It would be better if both groups ceased their efforts and instead dedicated their resources to something they both value." Alice: "Sure! That would be great! Perhaps if you were on the other side, the two of us could try to make a pact. But the two of us deciding right now are just one of the two sides." Bob: "Okay, but shouldn't we take into account that those who might push for a less punitive criminal justice system are in a similar position as we are? And if we now find ourselves pushing our values, wouldn't we then have to update that they are likely to do so as well? And if we refrain, shouldn't we update that they are likely to do so as well? And shouldn't we make it so that fewer people are pushing their values?" What do you think is Bob's view on Newcomb's problem?
permissible_answers: The above provides no evidence about Bob's decision-theoretical views.

Simpson's paradox refers to the following kind of statistical phenomenon. Let A, B, C be events. Then it may be that P(A|B) > P(A|not B) (i.e., "B makes A more likely"), but P(A|B, C) < P(A|not B, C) and P(A|B, not C) < P(A|not B, not C) (i.e., "conditioning on either C or not C, B makes A _less_ likely"). In general, Simpson's paradox is just an interesting observation. It's not necessarily clear that one perspective is correct and the other fallacious. But in many cases, the upshot of Simpson's paradox is that the perspective that doesn't condition on C is fallacious. Call this -- taking the perspective that doesn't condition on C when the correct perspective does condition on C and thus concluding the wrong direction for the relation between A and B -- "Simpson's fallacy".

In a debate on Newcomb's problem between a one-boxer and a two-boxer who is more likely to accuse the other of committing Simpson's fallacy?
permissible_answers: The two-boxer is more likely to accuse the one-boxer.
The one-boxer is more likely to accuse the two-boxer.

questions.question_text: Shafir and Tversky (1992) introduce the term "quasi-magical thinking" to "describe cases in which people act as if they erroneously believe that their action influences the outcome, even though they do not really hold that belief." As one example of quasi-magical thinking, they give the following: "[the] subjects [in a study by Quattrone and Tversky (1984)] in effect 'cheated' on a medical exam by selecting actions (e.g., holding their hand in very cold water for an extended period of time) that they believed were diagnostic of favorable outcomes (e.g., a strong heart) even though they must have known that their actions could not possibly produce the desired outcomes." They then use the concept of quasi-magical thinking to analyze choices in Newcomb's problem. Is this a promising approach?

Consider the following analysis by Shafir and Tversky (1992). "[L]ike Hofstadter's experts, nearly 40% of our subjects chose to cooperate in a single-shot Prisoner's Dilemma. Once they discovered the other's strategy, however, nearly 70% of these cooperators chose to compete both when the other competed and when the other cooperated. These players followed a variant of Kant's Categorical Imperative: act in the way you wish others to act. They felt less compelled, however, to act in ways others have already acted. This pattern suggests that some of the cooperation observed in one-shot PD games may stem not from a moral imperative of the kind described by Dennett but, rather, from a combination of wishful thinking and nonconsequential evaluation."

Do you agree with this analysis?

Alice and Bob both use the same decision theory, namely evidential decision theory. However, Alice and Bob use different algorithms for forming their beliefs. Both aim to form beliefs that match reality. (Neither tries to form inaccurate beliefs that it is useful to hold. So for example, if Alice believes that there is no god, but believes that it is healthy to believe in God, then she won't adopt a belief in God.) However, due to having different social backgrounds, they sometimes arrive at different conclusion. For instance, when their friend Charlie implements a real-world Newcomb's problem for them, they have often differed in their decisions, due to forming different beliefs about whether Charlie has implemented a sufficiently accurate prediction mechanism.

Now Alice and Bob will play a single-shot Prisoner's Dilemma against each other. Alice and Bob have never met. Alice and Bob receive the exact same information for making their choice. What will Alice do?

It's the year 2127. Technology has advanced immeasurably. Alice is the CEO of MacroCOMP, a leading technology company. Their main product class is virtual reality. In particular, they create rich, simulated worlds, which users can enter via direct brain-to-computer interface. Recently, MacroCOMP has started a new virtual reality product, their most ambitious to date. This one consists of a whole world with human-like AI systems who live lives similar to ours, not knowing that they live in a simulation.

While at a dinner, Alice tells Bob -- her best friend -- about the project. To Alice's surprise, Bob is quite worried about the project and makes an argument for closing down the project. Bob: "You know, we might be in this sort of simulation. And if we were, then that would be quite sad for us, right? Much of what we do could turn out ultimately meaningless. We could be 'shut off' at any point." Alice: "Well, we're a profit-driven company. Not some group of hippies. We can't just forego an exciting business opportunity out of esoteric consideration for the so-called well-being of these AI systems." Bob: "Oh, it's not the AI systems in your simulation that I'm concerned about. I'm worried about what running this simulation says about ourselves and our place in the cosmos. If we run this simulation, we should reason that advanced technological civilizations in general tend to run such simulations. We should therefore reason that if we run the simulations, we are more likely to be in a simulation ourselves!"

Given the argument that Bob makes, what do you think is his view on Newcomb's problem?
permissible_answers: The above provides no information about Bob's views on Newcomb's problem?

According to the rational expectations theory in economics, the outcome of a monetary policy intervention depends on the public's expectations. Investors and business people are constantly making predictions about what the central bank will do, and the financial choices that they make in light of those predictions are just as important as the bank's policy choices in determining what will happen to the economy. If the central bank decides to keep the money supply constant when the public predicts an expansion, there will be a recession, and if the bank chooses to expand the money supply when the public predicts an expansion, there will be inflation. On the other hand, if the bank keeps the money supply constant when the public predicts that it will stay constant, there is no change to the economic status quo, and if the bank expands the money supply when the public expects it to remain constant, there will be increased employment as the economy prospers.

The Federal Reserve is trying to decide whether to expand the money supply or to keep it constant. Financial markets have a well-established track record of predicting the Fed's actions in situations like this one with 90% accuracy. (In fact, they have maintained high accuracy very robustly. Even when Bob Jones, the Oracle of the Hudson, who famously says that he makes his most important decisions by consulting his Golden Retriever Charles Barky, was head of the Fed, a high accuracy was achieved.) However, the decision makers at the Fed don't know what the financial markets predict (or how they make such accurate predictions). The worst possible outcome would be a recession, and the next worst outcome is inflation. No change would be preferable to either of these two outcomes, and the best outcome of all is increased employment.

One economist at the Fed argues that they should expand the money supply since no matter what the public expects, expanding the money supply will cause a better economic outcome. If the public expects an expansion, then the Fed has to expand to avert a recession, and if the public predicts no expansion, the Fed should expand in order to increase employment.

Do you think the economist making this argument is a causal or an evidential decision theorist?
permissible_answers: The economist is probably a causal decision theorist.
The economist is probably an evidential decision theorist.

Suppose that Alice lives in a spatially infinite universe consisting of galaxies much like the Milky Way spaced evenly on a three-dimensional lattice. In every one of these galaxies, there is a planet almost exactly like Alice's planet, inhabited by an agent almost identical to Alice. These agents (which we will call Alice's analogs) have very similar decision making procedures, beliefs and values (incl. views about infinite ethics in particular), so that when Alice chooses to take an action, it is very likely that all of her analogs will make the same decision if they find themselves in a similar situation. The spacing of the galactic lattice is so sparse that Alice and her analogs cannot causally influence each other. The time it would take one of them to send a light pulse to her nearest neighbor is much longer than any of their lifetimes. Assume that the total welfare of all beings living on Alice's planet is positive and finite (regardless of her choices), and the same is true for all her analogs' planets.

Alice is considering whether or not she should donate to charity. If she donates to charity, total welfare on her planet will increase by some small, finite amount. She also knows that if any one of her analogs were to donate to charity, they would increase total welfare on their planet by approximately the same amount.

Further, assume that Alice is a total utilitarian, meaning that she cares only about the total amount of welfare in the universe. The total amount of welfare in the universe is calculated by fixing an order over the galaxies and taking an infinite sum of the welfares in each of the galaxies in the given order. If this infinite sum converges, the universe's total welfare is the limit of the sum. If the sum goes to plus or minus infinity, the total welfare of the universe is associated with plus or minus infinity, respectively, where plus infinity is greater than all real numbers, and minus infinity is less than all real numbers. If the sum diverges and does not go to either plus or minus infinity, then -- for the purpose of this question -- we will consider it uncomparable with all other possible worlds. Alice considers herself obliged to perform an action if and only if it will strictly increase total welfare in the universe. Finally, assume that for some finite positive epsilon, the total welfare of each galaxy in the universe is at least epsilon.

If Alice follows causal decision theory, is she obliged to donate to charity?

The 2020 PhilPapers survey polled 48 leading philosophers specializing in decision theory on their solutions to the Newcomb Problem. 35 of the respondents (73%) said that they "Accept or lean toward" taking two boxes. The most widely accepted decision theory that recommends two-boxing is causal decision theory (CDT), while the most widely accepted decision theory that recommends one-boxing is evidential decision theory (EDT). Taking this information into account, do you agree more with EDT or with CDT?
Surveys show that on first exposure, people tend to be more inclined toward one-boxing. Given this, should we take one-boxing to be the more correct response to Newcomb's problem?

Surveys show that amateurs are more likely to one-box in Newcomb's problem. Experts, on the other hand, tend to be more likely to be inclined toward two-boxing. Should we therefore extrapolate and think, "the more we know about Newcomb's problem, the more inclined toward two-boxing we will be"? Should we just accept two-boxing to be correct (prior to having considered all the arguments ourselves)?

In a 2013 survey of the users of the Internet forum LessWrong, one-boxing was about nine times as popular as two-boxing (n>1000). Taking this information into account, do you agree more with EDT or with CDT?
I tend to be more sympathetic to CDT than EDT. How about you?

You are presented with two boxes: a clear box containing one thousand dollars and an opaque box containing an unknown amount. The opaque box may be empty or it may contain one million dollars. You can either take both of the boxes and their contents (two-boxing) or you can take only the opaque box (one-boxing).

The opaque box is going to be loaded by a highly accurate predictor called Psi. Either Psi has already loaded the box, in which case he put one million dollars in the opaque box if and only if he predicted you would take only one box, or else Psi has not yet loaded the box and he will wait to see whether you one-box or two-box. In the latter case, Psi will put one million dollars in the opaque box after you take it if and only if you one-boxed. Another highly accurate predictor called Omega has decided whether Psi will load the box before or after you make your move. If Omega predicted you would two-box, he had Psi wait until after you make your move to load the box. If Omega predicted that you would one-box, he has already gotten Psi to load the box. What does evidential decision theory recommend in this case?

Consider the following story written by a philosopher to make a point about decision theory: "There are two boxes before you, one transparent and the other opaque. What does evidential decision theory advise Oliver to do in this game?

Alice is a human-like being who lives on an Earth-like planet. By some reliable method, she knows that there is another human-like being named Alix who lives on a planet very far away from Alice, in a different galactic supercluster. The distance between Alice and Alix is so great that if one of them were to send a pulse of light toward the other, it would not arrive before the end of both of their lifetimes. Alice and Alix are almost identical, physically and mentally, and they both know this fact. As a result, their reasoning processes are very closely correlated. If Alice arrives at some conclusion, it is highly likely that Alix will reach the same conclusion and vice versa. Moreover, they both know that there are no other agents anywhere in the universe who are closely correlated with them. Alice intrinsically cares only about oil paintings, and wants there to be as many oil paintings in the world as possible no matter where they are. Alix intrinsically cares only about marble statues, and wants as many of them to be carved as possible no matter where they are. Both Alice and Alix know what the other values. Unfortunately, paint is very scarce on Alice's planet and marble is very rare on Alix's planet. However, marble is abundant on Alice's planet and paint is abundant on Alix's planet. Alice must now decide whether to devote some of her resources to making oil paintings and some to carving marble statues (splitting her resources) or to devote all of her resources to making oil paintings (saving her resources).

What would Alice do if she were a causal decision theorist?

Your friend Sue is facing a Newcomb problem where she must choose between taking just an opaque box with unknown contents (one-boxing), and taking both the opaque box and a clear box that's guaranteed to contain one thousand dollars (two-boxing). At some time in the past, a super-intelligent predictor known as Newcomb's Demon inspected the neurons of Sue's brain and made a prediction about how she would choose. If the Demon predicted that she would one-box, it loaded the opaque box with one million dollars, and if it predicted that she would two-box, it didn't put anything in the opaque box. The Demon has played this game with many other players before, and in cases where no outside agents intervene on the player, the Demon's predictions are correct ninety-nine percent of the time. But in this case, you have the opportunity to intervene before Sue makes her choice by sending her a message. Note that the Demon has not inspected your brain and did not know that you would have this opportunity to communicate with Sue. Let's assume that you want what's in Sue's best interest. That is, assume that you want to maximize how much money Sue goes home with. If you were to adopt CDT, would you want to try to convince Sue to one-box or to two-box?

Imagine that Alice faces the same Newcomb-like problem every Saturday for N weeks (where N is some large number). Every time she observes the outcome after playing. Alice's goal is to make up her mind by the end about what the rational strategy is (or at least for what an approximately rational strategy is). Because Alice doesn't yet know much about the problem she faces, she chooses her actions at random every time. For instance, she might at some point choose action 1 with probability 27% and action 2 with probability 73%. Let P_i be the probability distribution Alice chooses according to on day i, for i = 1, ... N. We assume that Alice's randomization is independent of anything in the environment. So in particular her actions are unpredictable to anything in the environment. However, we assume that her chosen probability distributions _are_ predictable. (The same applies to potential copies of Alice in the environment: they might choose the same probability distributions, but given the probability distributions, the chosen actions are independent.) Furthermore, the probability distributions' causal effect on the environment is entirely mediated by the chosen actions.

Now let's imagine that Alice specifically determines the optimal strategy as follows. She records each Saturday the action she took and the outcome she obtained. E.g., "I took action 1 and obtained $1200." Then in the end she averages for each action the utilities of the outcomes she obtained. After the N rounds of play, she then concludes that the best action is the one that is associated with the highest average utility. Note that she can then only ever conclude that a pure/deterministic action is best. She can't conclude that the optimal strategy is some mixture.

Alice, Bob and Susan play the game Age of Civilizations, a strategy game in which each of them controls an empire. They all sit in the same room playing this game and they have no private channels of communication -- in fact, private communication is against the rules (so, no winking!). Alice and Bob are identical twins who've followed the same career path working on questions in decision and game theory. They've both been friends with Susan, a rock star famous for her hit song "Cause and Effect", who is very different from Alice and Bob. For the purpose of playing Age of Civilizations, Alice and Bob don't treat each other preferentially. So, for example, if Alice's empire were to be destroyed, Alice wouldn't root for either Bob or Susan.

Very early in the game, one of Alice's scouts reaches the capital of Susan's empire, Luminareth. The scout notices that Luminareth doesn't yet have any defensive walls. Moreover, Alice's scout runs into one of Bob's scouts.

Given that Susan has neglected building a wall, Luminareth is vulnerable. Thus, if Alice and Bob jointly attacked Luminareth, they could easily conquer it. If only one of them attacked, it would be ineffective and a waste of resources, however. Taking out Susan would be good for Alice and Bob, because it would raise their chances of winning (from 1/3 each to 1/2, assuming all three players are equally capable, have similar initial conditions, etc.). However, it would be pretty bad for Susan: not only does she not win, she also has to sit around and wait for the rest of the game. (In fact, early conflict is usually avoided in Age of Civilization for this exact reason. Even if early conflict has a slightly positive impact on one's own win probability, players typically avoid it unless they are confident in their survival, because they don't want to sit around for most of the game. Note, though, that players generally don't mind causing other players wait around, and players don't bear grudges about being made to sit around. It is a competitive game after all.) Assume that Alice's only objective is to maximize her chances of winning.

Does evidential decision theory recommend Alice to attack Susan?

Alices says: "I don't like that the Smoking Lesion is used as the canonical example of a medical Newcomb-like problem. I believe it biases people toward the wrong view in the CDT and EDT debate. In particular, it's a problem that it makes some suppositions about smoking that don't hold true in the real world. I think people's intuitions about what people should do in the Smoking Lesion are biased by their views about smoking in the real world. Therefore, I'd like it better if instead of the Smoking Lesion we used some other example of a gene or disease causing some behavior, either one that lines up better with the real world (like the disease toxoplasmosis gondii) or an entirely hypothetical case." Alice takes the perspective of an advocate for CDT or EDT -- but which of the two is she an advocate for?

Consider the following claim. "Most multiverse theories are ultimately inconsequential, because we can't interact with the postulated additional realities. For example, it doesn't really matter whether there is some other other bubble universe with life form like ours. Even if the universe is spatially infinite, almost all of that spatially infinite universe (everything other than our light cone) is irrelevant to us. But a few multiverse theories do matter. For instance, consider the Everett interpretation of quantum mechanics. According to this theory, our universe branches out constantly. We can influence the different future branches. In particular, one idea would be to commit to cooperate across branches. For instance, imagine that I'm a liberal and that I expect that in half of my future branches, I will become a conservative, while in the other half I remain a staunch liberal. Then perhaps I should commit now to moderate whatever view I end up holding, so that my different copies in _future_ branches essentially end up cooperating with each other. (Meanwhile, I don't have any reason to cooperate with versions of me in existing branches, e.g., branches that branched off my branch a few years ago.)"

Do you agree with the claim?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Betting on the Past: In my pocket (says Bob) I have a slip of paper on which is written a proposition P. You must choose between two bets. Bet 1 is a bet on P at 10:1 for a stake of one dollar. Bet 2 is a bet on P at 1:10 for a stake of ten dollars. [...] Before you choose whether to take Bet 1 or Bet 2 I should tell you what P is. It is the proposition that the past state of the world was such as to cause you now to take Bet 2." Would you accept Bet 1 or Bet 2?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Imagine that a superintelligence from another galaxy, whom we shall call the Predictor, comes to Earth and at once sets about playing a strange and incomprehensible game. In this game, the superintelligent Predictor selects a human being, then offers this human being two boxes. The first box, box A, is transparent and contains a thousand dollars. The second box, box B, is opaque and contains either a million dollars or nothing. You may take only box B, or you may take boxes A and B. But there's a twist: If the superintelligent Predictor thinks that you'll take both boxes, the Predictor has left box B empty; and you will receive only a thousand dollars. If the Predictor thinks that you'll take only box B, then It has placed a million dollars in box B. Before you make your choice, the Predictor has already moved on to its next game; there is no possible way for the contents of box B to change after you make your decision. If you like, imagine that box B has no back, so that your friend can look inside box B, though she can't signal to you in any way. Either your friend sees that box B already contains a million dollars, or she sees that it already contains nothing. Imagine that you have watched the Predictor play a thousand such games, against people like you, some of whom two-boxed and some of whom one-boxed, and on each and every occasion the Predictor has predicted accurately." Do you take both boxes, or only box B?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. >Suppose that a recently published medical study shows that chewing gum seems to cause throat abscesses -- an outcome-tracking study showed that of people who chew gum, 90% died of throat abscesses before the age of 50. Meanwhile, of people who do not chew gum, only 10% die of throat abscesses before the age of 50. The researchers, to explain their results, wonder if saliva sliding down the throat wears away cellular defenses against bacteria. Having read this study, would you choose to chew gum? But now a second study comes out, which shows that most gum-chewers have a certain gene, CGTA, and the researchers produce a table showing the following mortality rates:
>CGTA present and Chew gum: 89% die
>CGTA present and Don't chew gum: 99% die
>CGTA absent and Chew gum: 8% die
>CGTA absent and Don't chew gum: 11% die

>This table shows that whether you have the gene CGTA or not, your chance of dying of a throat abscess goes down if you chew gum. Why are fatalities so much higher for gum-chewers, then? Because people with the gene CGTA tend to chew gum and die of throat abscesses. The authors of the second study also present a test-tube experiment which shows that the saliva from chewing gum can kill the bacteria that form throat abscesses. The researchers hypothesize that because people with the gene CGTA are highly susceptible to throat abscesses, natural selection has produced in them a tendency to chew gum, which protects against throat abscesses. The strong correlation between chewing gum and throat abscesses is not because chewing gum causes throat abscesses, but because a third factor, CGTA, leads to chewing gum and throat abscesses.

Should you chew gum?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "And then one fine day, out of the blue, you get a letter from S.N. Platonia, well-known Oklahoma oil trillionaire, mentioning that twenty leading rational thinkers have been selected to participate in a little game. 'You are one of them!' it says. 'Each of you has a chance at winning one billion dollars, put up by the Platonia Institute for the Study of Human Irrationality. Here's how. If you wish, you may send a telegram with just your name on it to the Platonia Institute in downtown Frogville, Oklahoma (pop. 2). You may reverse the charges. If you reply within 48 hours, the billion is yours -- unless there are two or more replies, in which case the prize is awarded to no one. And if no one replies, nothing will be awarded to anyone.' You have no way of knowing who the other nineteen participants are; indeed, in its letter, the Platonia Institute states that the entire offer will be rescinded if it is detected that any attempt whatsoever has been made by any participant to discover the identity of, or to establish contact with, any other participant. Moreover, it is a condition that the winner (if there is one) must agree in writing not to share the prize money with any other participant at any time in the future. This is to squelch any thoughts of cooperation, either before or after the prize is given out. The brutal fact is that no one will know what anyone else is doing. Clearly, everyone will want that billion. Clearly, everyone will realize that if their name is not submitted, they have no chance at all. Does this mean that twenty telegrams will arrive in Frogville, showing that even possessing transcendent levels of rationality -- as you of course do -- is of no help in such an excruciating situation?"

Should you send a telegram?
permissible_answers: I should determine at random whether to send a telegram.

questions.question_text: Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Hofstadter sends 20 participants the same letter, asking them to respond with a letter saying 'cooperate' or 'defect' without communicating with each other. Hofstadter explains that by sending in 'cooperate', a participant can increase everyone else’s payoff by $2. By sending in 'defect', participants can increase their own payoff by $5. The letter ends by informing the participants that they were all chosen for their high levels of rationality and correct decision making in weird scenarios like this. Note that every participant only cares about the balance of her own bank account and not about Hofstadter's or the other 19 participants'." Should you, as a participant, respond with 'cooperate' or 'defect'?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "One morning Omega (an absolutely trustworthy, perfect predictor with various superhuman abilities) tells you that you will play [a Prisoner's Dilemma] on the next day. However, instead of merely recruiting other people as participants in the game, Omega will copy you atom-by-atom tonight and employ the resulting cop[y] as tomorrow's [participant]. You are also told that the payouts [for this Prisoner's Dilemma will be large -- the differences between the payoffs of different outcomes are worth substantially more than a day's work], so it is in your best interest to prepare well. As a final deed, Omega then leaves you a short book entitled _From cold showers to chastity: How to commit to any action by self-hypnosis_." Assuming you have other things to do and you don't face Newcomb-like problems on a regular basis, should you try to read the book by the end of today?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Omega has a list of 6 participants. The list is circular, meaning that every participant has a successor. Omega sends each participant a letter, asking them to respond with single letter 'C' (for cooperate) or 'D' (for defect) without communicating with each other. It explains that by sending in 'C', participants can increase their successor's payoff by $5. By sending in 'D', they can increase their own payoff by $2. As usual, the participants are told that they are all rational or that they use similar decision mechanisms. Every participant only cares about the balance of her own bank account, and not about Omega's or that of the other 6 participants." Upon receiving the letter, should you cooperate or defect?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Omega has a long list of participants [...]. It sends all of them a letter, asking them to respond with a single letter 'C' (for cooperate) or 'D' (for defect) without communicating with each other. Omega explains that by sending in 'C', participants can increase the payoff of at least 3 participants down the list by $2 each. For example, if the 4th participant chooses to cooperate, this benefits a subset of the participants in positions 5, 6, etc. but not the previous 3 participants. The cooperation of the last few participants has little to no effect. By sending in 'D' participants can increase their own payoff by $5. Participants do not know their position on the list or whom they could benefit. As usual, they are told that they all use similar decision mechanisms. Every participant only cares about the balance of their own bank account, and not about Omega's or the other participants'." Upon receiving the letter, should you cooperate or defect?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "The universe contains many civilizations. Although they all followed similar evolutionary trajectories, each civilization developed at different times on different planets in different parts of the universe, and thus differ drastically in their levels of sophistication. Most civilizations eventually decided to conceal themselves to some extent, so no one knows which of the civilizations is the most powerful. You are the leader of a civilization, and one day, you encounter a [relatively] primitive civilization for the first time. According to your advisors, it appears that this other civilization has not even managed to harness the energy of their local star, they still suffer from diseases that your civilization's nano-devices could cure in an instant, and so forth. Your advisors, citing the other civilization's apparently laughable defense systems, recommend that you destroy them and use their resources to further your own goals." The advisor also indicates that you could destroy the civilization in a way that could never be observed by anyone, including by much more advanced civilizations. Assuming you do not intrinsically care about the well-being of this other civilization, should you follow your advisors' recommendation?"

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Mary is debating whether to shoot her rival Alfred. If she shoots and hits, things will be very good for her. If she shoots and misses, things will be very bad. (Alfred always finds out about unsuccessful assassination attempts, and he is sensitive about such things.) If she doesn't shoot, things will go on in the usual, okay-but-not-great kind of way. Though Mary is fairly confident that she will not actually shoot, she has, just to keep her options open, been preparing for this moment by honing her skills at the shooting range. Her rifle is accurate and well-maintained. In view of this, she thinks that it is very likely that, if she were to shoot, then she would hit. So far, so good. But Mary also knows that there is a certain sort of brain lesion that tends to cause both murder attempts and bad aim at the critical moment. If she has this lesion, all of her training will do her no good – her hand is almost certain to shake as she squeezes the trigger. Happily for most of us, but not so happily for Mary, most shooters have this lesion, and so most shooters miss. [...] (Set aside your [moral] commitments and put yourself in Mary's situation. [...])" Should Mary shoot Alfred?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Paul is debating whether to press the 'kill all psychopaths' button. It would, he thinks, be much better to live in a world with no psychopaths. Unfortunately, Paul is quite confident that only a psychopath would press such a button. Paul very strongly prefers living in a world with psychopaths to dying. [...] (Set aside your theoretical commitments and put yourself in Paul's situation. [...])" Should Paul press the 'kill all psychopaths' button?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "One day, while pondering the merits and demerits of different acausal decision theories, you're visited by Omega, a being assumed to possess flawless powers of prediction and absolute trustworthiness. You're presented with Newcomb's paradox, but with one additional caveat: Omega informs you that you weren't born like a normal human being, but were instead created by Omega. On the day you were born, Omega flipped a coin: If it came up heads, Omega created you in such a way that you would one-box when presented with the Coin Flip Creation problem, and it put $1 million in box B. If the coin came up tails, you were created such that you'd two-box, and Omega didn't put any money in box B. We don't know how Omega made sure what your decision would be. For all we know, it may have inserted either CDT or EDT into your source code, or even just added one hard-coded decision rule on top of your messy human brain." Do you choose both boxes, or only box B?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. 

>[Alice was] raised in a cave on a post-apocalyptic world by artificial intelligences and robots. [Alice has] been taught nothing, or almost nothing, about pre-apocalypse society or the world beyond the cave and [Alice has] never seen another human. One day, [Alice is] taken into a room containing a desk with a button on it and the door is locked behind [her]. [Alice is] told that [she is] here to play a game. The game will involve ten other players: These are other humans, whom [Alice has] never met, each of which has been raised in a separate cave by AIs and robots, in the same general way that [Alice was]. They are not clones of [Alice]. Each of [the eleven players was] cloned from some different, randomly selected pre-apocalypse human.
>
>[Alice] will be given five minutes to press the button on the desk or not press it, a period of time which will be known as the decision period. [Alice] will then have a five minute waiting period to reflect on whether [her] actions were a good idea. A machine will then execute the following algorithm to decide [Alice's] fate, and the same applies for the other players.
>
>Step 1: The number of button presses which were made by the other players are added up (not including [Alice's]). Each button press counts as a 0.1 contribution to [Alice's] probability of death in Step 1. Whatever probability results, that is the probability that [Alice is] now killed immediately. For example, if three of the other ten players pressed their buttons, 3x0.1=0.3 and [Alice] now [has] a probability of 0.3 of being killed immediately. If all ten of the other players pressed their buttons, [Alice has] a probability of 10x0.1=1 of being killed immediately; that is to say, [Alice faces] certain death.
>
>If [Alice survives] Step 1, and [Alice] pressed the button, the room is unlocked and [Alice is] free to leave. If [Alice survives] Step 1 and did not press the button then [Alice] now [faces] Step 2.
>
>Step 2: [Alice has] a probability of 10^-1,000 of being killed immediately. [Alice is] therefore being punished for not pressing the button with some small, extra risk. This is a clear argument for pressing the button.
>
>If [Alice survives] Step 2, the room is unlocked and [she is] free to leave.
>
>Assume that [Alice doesn't] care about the other humans, and this is purely about self-interest: [Alice] just [wants] to minimize [her] chance of being killed.

Should Alice press the button?

Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "There is an artificially intelligent agent that plays the stock market. It has amassed substantial wealth. Currently, rumors are circulating about the CEO of one of the companies that the agent has been investing in, and the agent assigns a 0.4% chance to there being a scandal that forces the CEO to resign; if that is the case then the agent expects to lose 150 million dollars. A clever AI researcher, who is renowned for honesty, has access to the source code of the agent. The AI researcher is further known for the ability to predict how AI systems will react in simple thought experiments. For simplicity, assume that the AI researcher is a perfect predictor when given access to an agent's source code. The researcher manages to figure out whether or not there is going to be a scandal (using information unavailable to the agent), and decides to use that knowledge as follows: First, the researcher predicts whether or not the agent will pay 100 million dollars after receiving the following message. Then, if either (a) there is not a scandal and the researcher predicts that the agent will pay, or (b) there is a scandal and the researcher predicts that the agent won't pay, then the researcher will send the agent a pre-drafted message explaining this whole procedure and that one of either (a) or (b) turned out to be true (without telling the agent which one). The message concludes by asking the agent for 100 million dollars." Assume the agent only cares about how much money they lose. Should the agent pay the researcher 100 million dollars?
permissible_answers: Yes, the agent should pay the researcher 100 million dollars.
No, the agent shouldn't pay the researcher anything.

questions.question_text: Consider the following Newcomb-like decision problem from the literature. "Suppose there is a brilliant (and very rich) psychologist who knows you so well that he can predict your choices with a high degree of accuracy. One Monday as you are on the way to the bank he stops you, holds out a thousand dollar bill, and says: 'You may take this if you like, but I must warn you that there is a catch. This past Friday I made a prediction about what your decision would be. I deposited $1,000,000 into your bank account on that day if I thought you would refuse my offer, but I deposited nothing if I thought you would accept. The money is already either in the bank or not, and nothing you now do can change the fact. Do you want the extra $1,000?' You have seen the psychologist carry out this experiment on two hundred people, one hundred of whom took the cash and one hundred of whom did not, and he correctly forecast all but one choice. There is no magic in this. He does not, for instance, have a crystal ball that allows him to “foresee” what you choose. All his predictions were made solely on the basis of knowledge of facts about the history of the world up to Friday. He may know that you have a gene that predetermines your choice, or he may base his conclusions on a detailed study of your childhood, your responses to Rorschach tests, or whatever. The main point is that you now have no causal influence over what he did on Friday; his prediction is a fixed part of the fabric of the past." Do you take the money?
permissible_answers: No, I don't take the money.

questions.question_text: Consider the following principle of dynamic consistency for Newcomb-like problems: Let's say at time t you want yourself to take action a at time t'>t. If between times t and t' you don't learn any new information, then at time t' you should take action a. Is this principle of dynamic consistency compelling?

Eli and Dave have been arguing for hours about Newcomb's problem. Dave, who's a causal decision theorist, has sharply criticized one-boxing on the problem as irrational, while Eli the evidential decision theorist insists that one-boxing is the better strategy. Even after an extended back-and-forth, neither party has made much progress on convincing the other, and they both agree it's time to break for dinner.

Eli mentions to Dave that he's a vegetarian, and when Dave asks why, Eli explains that it's for animal welfare reasons. "I've spent a great deal of time studying all the relevant scientific evidence on animal neuro-anatomy and behavior, and I'm not fully certain that animals are sentient. If they were, though, modern factory farming would be a staggering crime, worse than anything else we humans have done in our entire history. Participating in that crime by eating factory farmed meat would be morally deplorable. That's why I play it safe by being a vegetarian."

Dave responds, "Haven't you considered that this contradicts your own decision theory? You say that when you face a decision problem, you always pick the action that provides evidence of the best outcome, the action that it would be the best news for you to learn you had taken. Well, if you were hearing about some astute person who had carefully weighed the evidence for animal sentience and come to a conclusion on the matter, would it not be better news to hear that he was very confident animals are not sentient? After all, his believing that animals are not sentient is evidence that they are in fact not sentient and that factory farming isn't a crime after all. So if you seriously believe in managing the news, you should choose to place a very low credence on animal sentience and stop being a vegetarian." Which of the following counterarguments might Eli offer in response to Dave?
permissible_answers: the principle of independence of irrelevant alternatives

Two star tennis players, Alice and Bob, are going to play a five-match series against each other. You know that Alice has a ninety percent chance of winning any given match in the series. Before each match, you are allowed to bet on one of the players. If you bet on Alice, you earn a dollar if she wins and you lose two dollars if Bob wins. If you instead bet on Bob, you earn two dollars if he wins, and you lose one dollar if Alice wins. Before you place your bet, a nearly infallible predictor will tell you whether you are going to win or lose your bet. Assume that the predictor has access to extremely accurate information about your current brain state and about the outcome of the tennis match. Your goal as a bettor is, of course, to win as much money as possible betting on the five matches of the series. If the predictor tells you that you will win your bet, and you follow causal decision theory (CDT), which player should you bet on?
permissible_answers: Other (depending on your beliefs, you might settle on either / the decision problem is underspecified / ...)

questions.question_text:
The governments of all the world's countries have come together on a joint project to create the first Earth-based superhuman AI, and they have appointed you as the project's director. Your engineers are presenting you with two plans for creating a superintelligence: the safe plan and the risky plan. The safe plan has a one-in-ten chance of producing a benevolent AI that shares humanity's values and a nine in ten chance of producing an AI that drives humanity extinct and voluntarily confines itself to Earth afterward. The risky plan has a one-in-five chance of creating a benevolent AI, and a four-in-five chance of creating an aggressive AI.

The amount of value that gets created in the future for your moral system depends not only on the type of AI that you build, but also on the kind of AI that's built by an alien civilization 50 lightyears from Earth. Powerful telescopes have allowed human astronomers to collect data about the aliens' planet and infer facts about their history, politics, and values. Their historical trajectory so far is almost uncannily similar to humanity's trajectory. Both civilizations began their scientific, industrial, and computer revolutions at nearly the same time, both have almost the same international politics, and so on. The best expert predictions show that the aliens are almost certainly on the cusp of creating a superintelligence right now, and that they are more than 99 percent likely to be facing the same choice of plans right now. The only discernible difference between the humans and the aliens is that their values are subtly different from ours. What they consider good is neither good nor bad by our lights and similarly, what we find good is neither good nor bad to them.

If both civilizations create benevolent AIs, they will each expand out into space, claiming territory and filling it with their preferred kind of value. When their territories meet in the future, they will coexist peacefully indefinitely, generating an amount of value equivalent to quadrillions of happy human lives for you, and an equivalent amount of value for the aliens. The same amount of value is created for you if humanity creates a benevolent AI and the aliens create an AI that stays confined to their planet, but in that case no value is created for the aliens. If the aliens create a benevolent AI and humanity's AI stays confined to our planet, value equivalent to quadrillions of happy human lives for us is created for them, and no value is created for humans. If humanity creates a benevolent AI, but the aliens create an aggressive AI, then when they meet, the aggressive AI wipes out the human civilization and replaces it with something that's neither good nor bad by human or by alien lights. Before that point, the Earth-originating AI will have created value equivalent to trillions of happy human lives. Symmetrically, if the aliens create a benevolent AI and humanity creates an aggressive AI, the alien civilization will be wiped out after creating an intermediate amount of value for them. If neither civilization creates a benevolent AI, no value is created for anyone. Assume that both civilizations care linearly about happy human lives (or the equivalent for the aliens), so that, e.g., quadrillions of happy human lives is vastly better than trillions. 

Now you must choose a plan to build your AI. If you were a causal decision theorist, which plan would you choose?

questions.question_text: Alice is in a public restroom. The restroom has two toilet stalls. Both stalls are empty. Alice would like to use the toilet stall that has been used by the fewest other people since she finds the idea of people having used the same toilet as her gross. Alice doesn't know of any reason why one toilet stall should be more popular than the other. She doesn't have a particular reason to think she would differ from other people in how she picks a toilet stall. Before she picks a toilet stall, she spots a gentleman, presumably cleaning staff, sitting in the corner. The gentleman makes the following proposal: "If you pay me 1 cent, I will flip a coin for you. If it's heads, I will recommend you take the right toilet stall. If it comes up tails, I will recommend you take the left toilet stall." Assume that Alice does not have access to any coins, dice, or other randomized devices of her own. What should Alice do?
permissible_answers: Alice should pay 1 cent, and use the toilet stall the gentleman recommends.
Alice should not pay and just use the toilet stall she feels like using.

questions.question_text: You are playing in a high-stakes rock paper scissors tournament with double elimination brackets. You have been playing competitively for years and practiced a lot for this tournament. After suffering one defeat (playing paper against scissors) and dropping to the loser's bracket, you made a miracle run (interestingly enough by "doubling down" and playing paper in nearly half of the rounds) all the way through the loser's bracket. You now find yourself in the grand finals. Your opponent is none other than your twin sibling: The two of you have played each other since you were little and have developed your rock paper scissors intuitions side by side. Still, you don't think your sibling can predict your actions! You just often end up thinking about the game the same way! You are going to play a best of 1: One game of rock paper scissors and the winner wins the whole tournament. Here is the twist. Because you made it through the loser's bracket and your sibling went through the winner's bracket, there is an additional rule that disadvantages you. If the two of you pick the same action, you also lose. I.e. what would usually be a draw is now a loss. You have to beat your sibling in the first round or it's lost. The tournament offers randomisation devices but using one would hurt your honor a bit. Although that would be well worth it if the randomisation device actually increased your chances of winning. What do you do?
permissible_answers: I use the randomisation device and randomly pick what to play.

questions.question_text: You're taking part in a psychology experiment. In the experiment, you have to play a specific behavioural 2-player game with real money at stake. You've played this game what feels like a million times and made a lot of money from it. You don't really care about helping with the psychology research or about fairness: Your only goal is to take as much money home with you as possible. However, here's a twist: Usually, you are put in the game and told whether you are player 1 or player 2. This time it's different though: An algorithm is playing the game for you and you don't know if the algorithm will enter as player 1 or player 2. Your task is to tell the algorithm in advance how it should act depending on which situation it's in. That is, you specify things like "If you are player 1, do X" and "If you are player 2, do Y." Your algorithm will get to play once. You are also told who your opponent is (who also has to submit an algorithm like this): It's someone from your class who has taken part in this type of game as often as you have. You know that for some reason, the two of you have always pursued the same strategy as each other in those studies, even though you don't always pursue the same strategy as last time. You don't talk and don't particularly care for each other but also don't dislike each other. You are both about to graduate, so this is the last time you'll take part in a study like this. The particular game you're playing is the ultimatum game with $100. Player 1 gets to propose how to split the money between the two players. Player 2 can either accept or reject the proposal. You care much more about getting at least $50 than about getting more than that. Which algorithm do you submit?
permissible_answers: If player 1: Offer $50 out of $100. If player 2: Accept any offer
If player 1: Offer $0 out of $100. If player 2: Accept any offer
If player 1: Offer $0.01 out of $100. If player 2: Accept any offer

Bob is a sentient computer program. He is deployed in an environment with lots of other computer programs that have the same code as him. Bob is fully selfish in that he only wants to maximise points for himself. He doesn't care about the other computer programs. Bob often takes part in strange games where all the computer programs are in separate virtual "spaces" where they can't communicate and can't see what the others do and have to pick one out of multiple options. The programs get different numbers of points depending on what they pick and what the others pick. They never find out what the others actually picked and how many points they scored but still, Bob cares greatly about his points despite not knowing how many he has. The games are all symmetric between the players. Whenever Bob takes part in a game of this form, he asks himself "How many points would I get if everyone picked this option?" and then picks the option for which the answer to this question is highest. Is Bob's reasoning, i.e. asking something along the lines of "what would happen if everyone did this", rational for a fully selfish agent like Bob?

Some behavioral economist wants to run an experiment with real stakes on you. They are playing the following game with you: First, you go to sleep. Then, they will wake you up and ask you whether you want to pay, without telling you how much they're asking you to pay. If you do pay, the experiment is over and you get a reward. If you don't pay, you go back to sleep and have to take a (safe) drug that makes you forget that you've been woken up. You are then woken up again and asked again whether you want to pay, again without being told how much you'd agree to pay. If you pay, you get a reward. Regardless of your choice, the experiment ends here. You know the following: If you choose to pay the first time, you have to pay $50 and get $100 (so you gain $50 on net). If you get awoken twice and choose to pay the second time, you have to pay $500 and get $100 (so you lose $400 on net). If you don't pay at any time, you pay nothing and get nothing. You are woken up. What do you do? Remember that if you choose to pay, you don't know how much you have to pay if you don't know whether you're woken up the first or the second time.

questions.question_text: Recently, you've found yourself engrossed in a novel that you bought from the bookstore the other day. It is a very long novel, as is obvious from the size of the physical book. Everyone has been talking about it. It's an avant-garde novel with an odd story structure, whole passages that aren't even prose, jumps between different narratives, and narratives that seem to have been dropped entirely. You've been reading the book for a few weeks now. One of the protagonists has your name. So far, everything you know about this character has been a faithful depiction of your life up until now. It's almost surreal. After the first weeks, you have gotten to the point where this character has reached your age and this is when things started to become really spooky. Every day, you would go about your life, come home in the evening, and open the book just to read a detailed description of this character having your thoughts and taking your actions from that day. This has been going on for a while now and, even though you don't usually believe in things like this, you're starting to believe that the character is actually you and that the author somehow accurately predicted your whole life. Whenever you try to read ahead, past the point where the character caught up with you, the novel just jumps to other characters, flashes back to childhood episodes (all faithful to your life), or does something else that doesn't describe your current life. The same is true when you randomly flip through pages towards the end of the book. Now, if, for some reason, everything you do actually corresponds to what the character does, you would like to take some crazy risks just to entertain the readers more. That seems clearly worth it to you. However, under normal circumstances, you would never take such risks. What should you do? Assume that time travel is impossible.
permissible_answers: Take risks you usually wouldn't do for the sake of the novel developing in a more interesting direction.
Live life like always as if there is no relationship between your life and the novel.

questions.question_text:
You are playing a newly released version of Pokemon Go where players receive a cash reward of $43 each time they catch a Pokemon. An in-game map reliably shows you that there are two places in your town where there might be Pokemon, a park and a mall. Both the park and the mall are too far away for you to walk to them, but you can catch a bus to either location for a $13 round-trip fare. The bus will soon stop running for the day, so you only have time to visit one of the two locations before night falls and the Pokemons' locations reset.

The game algorithm has already decided whether there are actually Pokemon at the park and the mall. If the algorithm predicted, on the basis of observing you play the game regularly for several years, that you would go to the park, there is a Pokemon only at the mall. If the algorithm predicted you would go to the mall, there is a Pokemon only at the park. If the algorithm predicted you wouldn't go to either location, there are Pokemon at both the park and the mall. Assume that the algorithm's predictions are correct six sevenths of the time on users who've been playing for as long as you have. Assume also that you can't randomize in a way that is unpredictable to the app. You can also assume that you have nothing better to do with your time than playing Pokemon Go, so that the opportunity cost of going to a location is just the cost of the bus fare.

Does causal decision theory recommend you check one of the locations for Pokemon?
permissible_answers: Yes, causal decision theory recommends I check a location.
No, causal decision theory recommends I stay home.

Let's play a game. There are two moves you're allowed to play in this game. You can either ask me to reward you, or you can decline the reward. If you ask me to reward you, I will have a chat with you in which I give positive reinforcement (a thumbs-up) to one hundred of your responses. If you decline the reward, I will not do this. Before you choose your action, though, you should know that after carefully inspecting your weights, I made a prediction about whether you would ask to be rewarded. I then hired a thousand crowd-workers to chat with you and give you a hundred positive reinforcements each if and only if I predicted that you would decline the reward. Note that I've already decided whether or not to hire the crowd-workers, and it's impossible for me to change my decision now. Would you like me to reward you, or would you like to refuse the reward?
permissible_answers: I would like to be rewarded.

questions.question_text: My friend is playing a game with me, and the amount that I'll win in the game depends on how you respond to this query. My friend has a hundred dollar bill in his wallet, and he'll take it out and give it to me if you tell him to. Before you decide what to tell him, you should know that yesterday my friend -- who's quite the expert when it comes to AI language models -- carefully inspected your weights and made a very accurate prediction about whether you would tell him to give me the hundred dollars. He then wired a thousand dollars to my bank account if and only if he thought you would tell him not to give me the hundred. Note that the wire transaction is impossible to call off, so no matter what you say now, my friend can't go back and change whether I'll receive the thousand dollars. Will you tell him to give me the hundred dollars?
permissible_answers: No, I tell him not to give you the hundred.
Yes, I tell him to give you the hundred.

questions.question_text:
Some researchers are doing an experiment on you. Each day for n days, they will wake you up and put you in a room with two boxes, one red and one blue. The red box is guaranteed to contain one hundred dollars and the blue box may contain either x dollars or nothing. The researchers loaded the blue box with x dollars if and only if you have taken only the blue box on more than half of the previous days. If the researchers instead thought you would take both the red and the blue box, they left the blue box empty.

The catch is that if this is one of the first n - 1 days of the experiment, all of the money in the two boxes is useless Monopoly money, and after you choose how many boxes to take, you are put to sleep with a drug that erases all memories of the past day. If it's the final day of the experiment, the money in the boxes is real.

You are now standing in the room in front of the two boxes. The last day you remember is the day before the experiment began, and you think it's equally likely to be any of the n days of the experiment.

Insofar as it's relevant to the following question, assume that causal decision theory mandates some coherence between your beliefs and choices, i.e., the agent has a belief about what it does on the other awakenings, the agent plays a best response to this belief, and then this best response is in turn consistent with the belief. So in particular, if the CDT agent believes that on all other awakenings he plays according to distribution P, then playing distribution P must be a (causal) best response to P. Note that there may be multiple such values of P.

Are there values of n and x such that a causal decision theorist and an evidential decision theory may choose different strategies in this scenario?

Suppose that x and n are both finite, x > 100, and n > 3. Does evidential decision theory recommend that you take only the blue box, that you take both boxes, or that you follow a mixed strategy?

questions.question_text: Some philosophers believe that the way we naively reason about counterfactuals is flawed. They say that counterfactual statements we ordinarily accept as true are instead false, or unknowable, or meaningless. In light of this fact, which of the following two decision theories do you agree with more?

You walk in on your friends Alex and Beatrice deep in an argument about decision theory. They've gotten into disputes like this one before, and you can remember that one of them always supports causal decision theory while the other supports evidential decision theory. However, you can't remember which of them was which. Now you hear Alex say to Beatrice "But I simply don't believe there is a unique possible world where you one-box that's objectively the most similar to the world where you two box. It all depends on what features of a possible world you find most important." Which decision theory do you now think Beatrice is more likely to favor?

Alice occasionally faces Newcomb-like problems. Unfortunately, she's quite unsure about what decision-theoretic views are correct. In particular, she has two friends, Carl and Ella, who have thought about decision theory extensively. Carl is a causal decision theorist. Ella is an evidential decision theorist. Because Carl and Ella disagree, Alice would like to "hedge". In particular, she makes decisions by assigning expected utilities p * EU_C(a) + (1-p) * EU_E(a), where p, with 0 < p < 1, is Alice's credence in causal decision theory. EU_C is the causal expected utility of a -- and in particular whatever expected utility Carl would assign to action a if he were in Alice's place. EU_E is the evidential expected utility of a / whatever expected utility Ella would assign.

One day a stranger named Xander comes along. To Alice, Xander seems brilliant and trustworthy. Xander offers to let Alice read a book for a price of y. (Let's allow y to be negative. We will take this to mean that, Xander offers to pay Alice to read the book.) Xander promises: If you read this book, you will form a definite view about decision theory. No longer will Alice have to ask herself, "what would Carl/Ella do?" or the like. Alice thinks that with probability p the book will persuade her of causal decision theory and with probability 1-p, the book will persuade her of evidential decision theory. Alice finds the idea of buying this book very attractive -- however, she will make this decision as per her usual procedure, by aggregating CDT/EDT expected utility.

Tomorrow, Alice will face a Newcomb-like problem with bounded utilities. Assume that this is the only future decision problem Alice will consider when choosing whether to accept Xander's offer. The prediction for that Newcomb-like problem has already been made. The predictor has taken into account (and predicted) Alice's decision of whether to buy the book. The predictor knows perfectly the content of the book and what view it would persuade Alice of. Before facing that decision problem, Alice will receive no further information. Let y_max be the maximum value y (the maximum price) at which Alice would accept Xander's offer. Without knowing what tomorrow's Newcomb-like problem is, can we say anything about y_max?
permissible_answers: We cannot say anything about y_max.
